Road Hopper

The Great Equalizer — As Told by Sal "Pixel" Martinez

I knew Road Hopper was special the first Saturday morning it was on the floor. By ten AM there were kids lined up around the block. Not an exaggeration — around the block. I had Mrs. Gutierrez from the bakery next door come over and ask me if I was giving something away for free. I told her yeah, humiliation. Everybody got that for free.

Road Hopper was the great equalizer. I watched five-year-olds and forty-year-olds be equally terrible at it. Something about that little frog just broke people's brains. You'd see grown adults leaning their whole body to the right trying to make the frog jump further, like the cabinet could feel them shifting their weight. Dads who came in acting all cool, saying "I got this, I played the original" — splattered on the first highway. Every single time.

The line got so bad I had to institute a house rule: three lives, then move along. People grumbled, sure. But it was either that or fistfights. One Saturday the line went out the door, down the sidewalk, past the bakery, past the dry cleaner. Mrs. Gutierrez brought out a tray of conchas for the kids waiting in line. That woman was a saint.

The day I had to write out the house rules and tape them to the cabinet was a turning point for me. Not because of the rules — because it meant people cared enough to need rules. My little arcade in a strip mall off Route 9 had a line out the door. I still get choked up thinking about it.
